title: Standard infection control precautions
blurb: The ten everyday precautions you use for every patient, every time, and why contaminated gloves never leave the clinical zone.
question: At the end of an appointment, a colleague carries the used instrument tray down the corridor in her treatment gloves, presses the lift button and then stops at reception to write in the patient's notes. Which precautions has she broken, and what should she have done instead?

teach.body: Standard infection control precautions (SICPs) are the basic steps used for every patient, whether or not they are known to have an infection. People can carry blood-borne viruses such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV without knowing it, and a medical history only tells you what the patient knows and chooses to share. So you can't sort patients into 'safe' and 'risky'. Instead, you treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious and apply the same precautions to everyone.

teach.caption: These come from the National Infection Prevention and Control Manual for England. HTM 01-05 sets out how they apply to decontamination in dental practice.

teach.body: SICPs are the foundation. When a patient is known or suspected to have an infection that spreads in a particular way, such as a respiratory infection, transmission-based precautions (TBPs) are added on top. These might mean delaying routine treatment, seeing the patient at the end of the session, or wearing a respirator for an aerosol-generating procedure, as set out in a risk assessment. TBPs never replace SICPs; they are layered on top of them.

teach.h: Contaminated gloves stay in the clinical zone
teach.body: Treatment gloves are covered in invisible saliva and blood. If you wear them in the corridor, you leave micro-organisms on door handles, lift buttons, phones, patient notes and the reception desk, where people touch them with bare hands. Gloves protect you during the task; they then become a source of contamination. Take them off and clean your hands before you touch anything outside the clinical zone.

items: SICPs apply to every patient, because carriers may not know or declare an infection.
Ten elements: risk assessment, hand hygiene, cough hygiene, PPE, equipment, environment, linen, spills, waste, exposure.
TBPs are added on top of SICPs for known or suspected infection.
Never wear treatment gloves outside the clinical zone; remove them and clean your hands.
Move used instruments in a rigid, lidded box.

summary: You can now explain why the same precautions are used for every patient, list the ten standard infection control precautions, tell SICPs and transmission-based precautions apart, and keep contamination inside the clinical zone by removing gloves and using lidded boxes.

A.q: Why are standard infection control precautions used for every patient, not just those who report an infection?
options: Carriers may not know or say
It saves time on medical histories
The law bans asking about infections
A.why: People can carry blood-borne viruses without symptoms or without telling you, so you can't rely on the medical history to identify them.

whyNot.0: Most patients are not infectious; you simply can't tell which ones are.
whyNot.2: A medical history is still taken; SICPs add to it rather than replace it.
whyNot.3: You can and should ask about infections in the medical history.

A.q: After treatment, a dental nurse walks the patient to reception still wearing her treatment gloves. What is the main problem?
options: The gloves may tear on the desk edge
It wastes a pair of gloves
A.why: Used gloves carry saliva and blood, so anything touched at reception becomes contaminated for others who touch it bare-handed.

whyNot.0: Anxiety isn't the main concern; spreading contamination is.
whyNot.1: Tearing is not the issue; the gloves are already contaminated.
whyNot.2: Waste is a minor point compared with spreading micro-organisms.

A.q: Which of these is NOT one of the standard infection control precautions?
A.why: Prescribing antibiotics is a treatment decision, not an infection control precaution, and it is outside a dental nurse's scope.

whyNot.1: Respiratory and cough hygiene is one of the ten SICPs.
whyNot.2: Safe management of linen, including uniforms, is one of the ten SICPs.
whyNot.3: Safe disposal of waste, including sharps, is one of the ten SICPs.

B.q: A patient in the waiting room is coughing and sneezing. Which SICP is most relevant?
B.why: Respiratory and cough hygiene means offering tissues, a bin and hand hygiene so droplets aren't spread to others.

whyNot.0: Linen management covers uniforms and towels, not coughs.
whyNot.1: Sharps disposal has nothing to do with a coughing patient.
whyNot.3: Equipment management covers cleaning and reprocessing care equipment.

B.q: A nurse writes in a patient's paper record while still wearing contaminated gloves. What is the main concern?
B.why: Micro-organisms on the gloves transfer to the notes, which other staff will later handle without gloves.

whyNot.1: The gloves being damaged is not the issue.
whyNot.2: Handwriting is not an infection control concern.
whyNot.3: Writing in the notes is not a confidentiality breach in itself.

B.why: TBPs are added on top of SICPs when a patient is known or suspected to have an infection that needs extra control.

whyNot.0: Every routine patient receives SICPs; TBPs are only added when needed.
whyNot.1: TBPs never replace SICPs; they are layered on top.
whyNot.2: TBPs relate to patients with infections, not to a particular room.

C.q: Used instruments need to travel from the surgery to the decontamination room along a corridor. What is the safest approach?
options: Carry the open tray in used gloves
Wrap the tray in a paper towel
Wear used gloves to open the doors
Carry them in a lidded, rigid box
C.why: A rigid, lidded box contains the contamination, so you can remove your gloves, clean your hands and open doors safely.

whyNot.0: An open tray and used gloves both spread contamination to the corridor.
whyNot.1: A paper towel is not a secure, rigid container and won't stop leaks or sharps.
whyNot.2: Used gloves contaminate door handles for everyone who touches them.

C.q: What does 'standard' mean in standard infection control precautions?
options: Applied to every patient, every time
Carried out by the dentist only
C.why: Standard precautions are the baseline used for all patients in all care, regardless of known infection status.

whyNot.0: That describes transmission-based precautions, which are added for specific infections.
whyNot.2: The whole team follows SICPs, not just the dentist.
whyNot.3: SICPs apply to every procedure, from check-ups to extractions.

C.q: Which SICP covers cleaning the dental chair and work surfaces between patients?
C.why: Safe management of the care environment means keeping surfaces and fixtures clean between patients.

whyNot.0: Linen management covers uniforms and towels.
whyNot.1: Patient placement is about where and when an infectious patient is seen.
whyNot.3: Occupational exposure management covers sharps injuries and splashes to staff.

reteach.title: Seatbelts on every journey
reteach.question: You wear a seatbelt on every journey, not only the ones where you expect a crash. How is that like standard infection control precautions?

blocks.body: Nobody knows in advance which car journey will end in a crash, so you buckle up every time. Infection control works the same way. You can't tell which patient carries hepatitis B or HIV, because they may look and feel well and may not know themselves. So the same basic precautions go on for every patient, every time. If you know there's ice on the road, you also slow down: that is like adding transmission-based precautions for a known infection.

steps.label: Safe sharps and waste
steps.sub: Right bin, at the point of use

blocks.text: 'Low-risk patient' is not a reason to cut corners. SICPs are the minimum for everyone.

explain.body: SICPs apply to every patient because infections can't be identified reliably from appearance or history. TBPs are added on top when an infection is known or suspected.

test.q: A patient reports no medical conditions at all. Which precautions should you use?
options: Precautions only if blood is seen
test.why: Every patient receives standard precautions; an empty medical history doesn't prove the patient is free of infection.

whyNot.1: There is no reduced level; SICPs are the minimum.
whyNot.2: Saliva can contain blood you can't see, and precautions start before treatment.
whyNot.3: TBPs are only added for known or suspected infection.

explain.body: Risk assessment, hand hygiene, respiratory and cough hygiene, PPE, care equipment, care environment, linen, blood and body fluid spills, waste, and occupational exposure (including sharps).

test.q: Which of these is one of the ten standard infection control precautions?
test.why: Safe management of blood and body fluid spillages is one of the ten SICPs.

whyNot.0: Fluoride varnish is a preventive treatment, not an infection control precaution.
whyNot.1: Radiation protection is covered by IRR17 and IR(ME)R, not SICPs.
whyNot.3: Emergency drills are part of medical emergency training.

explain.body: Used gloves contaminate everything they touch. Remove them and clean your hands before leaving the clinical zone, and carry used instruments in a rigid, lidded box.

test.q: A colleague presses the lift button in examination gloves while carrying used instruments. What is the main issue?
test.why: Contaminated gloves leave micro-organisms on the lift button, which others then touch with bare hands.

whyNot.0: Splitting is not the problem here; contamination is.
whyNot.2: Glove use has no effect on the lift working.
whyNot.3: Dropping is a risk, but the breach is touching surfaces with contaminated gloves.
